Laura:

You raise several good questions, let me intersperse my thoughts following each question:

On 30/06/2015 16:02, Laura Secada wrote:
>
> Thank you Eric for very clear and helpful answers. I am afraid more questions have arised as I explore my data. I am sorry questions are a mix between cluster size, heaping at cero distance, entry data and interpretation of Distance analysis results.
>
>
> Cluster size/ungrouped data
>
> I have read that loose population patterns such as the deer population in my study area are more difficult to model, I am not sure why is this. For example I have average cluster size is 1.46 and correlation  0.0499. I decided to try running analysis using cluster size and the ungrouped data.  When I run with cluster size it ran ok but a soon as I marked the density output option a warning message appeared** Warning: Size bias adjustment has increased expected cluster size. **
>
> When I ran ungrouped data with it came green light without truncation then 150m came ok as well and when I tried with 100m it came a warning light ** Warning: Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity. ** When I ran with 50m it came out green again, this is the smallest AIC I´ve got 1937.33
>
>

Loose animal aggregations make estimating group size difficult.  The expected pattern of data collected in the field is that small groups of animals are likely to be undetected at large distances; consequently the average size of detected groups *overestimates* the average group size in the population (the size bias problem).  Distance attempts to correct for size bias using regression; in your case Distance has alerted you to the fact that for your data, the regression adjustment has increased rather than decreased expected group size in the population.

Binning (or grouping) your distances need only be performed when the recorded exact distances are suspect (perhaps see below).  The monotonicity message is simply a report that Distance has fitted a model where detection probability continues to decrease as perpendicular distance increases; although your data show a pattern wherein there are elevated numbers of detections at some large distances.  Not an error, simply a report.

> severe ‘spike’ at 0 distance
>
> Previously when I analysed frequency histograms with same intervals I noticed heaping in cero distance the same with Qqplot where I have a qq plot, showing a severe ‘spike’ at 0 distance. heaping at cero distance  can this be improved my left truncation? I suspect that the case is that in this 10 year study with volunteers, sometimes they spot a deer in the trail and assume its distance 0 and they dont follor the same protoco as for other sightings so they just say it´s 0m. It mught well be distance 0 at the end but I am recommending they should take distance to observer and bearing and then calculate perpendicular distance as we do with rest of data. I think this will come with less ceros and more in between 10-20m perp distance from the line. But for now how can I improve the skipe at cero distance and how does a spike affect Distance.

This is an unpleasant situation that you have inherited from the preceding 10 years of data collection.  Your diagnosis of the problem (observers rounding detections to zero because it was near the trail) is a common difficulty.  If the spike is real, i.e. detectability really does fall rapidly at short distances from the transect, then you need a model that attempts to fit the spike.  On the other hand, if the spike is artificial and caused by rounding, then a model that does not try to fit the spike (such as a half-normal) is the better option (but will fit the observed data poorly).  The decision will have to be taken based on opinion rather than data.  Clever analysis is not the remedy to this problem, improved field procedures are the remedy.

>
>  Data entry
>
> In relation to data entry, First, when I uploaded my data it automatically defined the column cluster size as a decimal, and don´t allowed me to change this to integer. I have seen in the user guide that this column can be integer, I was just curious if it is ok lo leave it this way as a decimal
>
> I was wondering if it is rifght to add new fields with no data for diatance and cluster size when the transect was visited and there was no sighting?

This was answered in a previous email.

> Recommended 2010 paper
>
> Second, I read the paper Buckland et al 2010 but I could´nt find reference to bias of ungrouped data.

Examine Table III that presents percent bias of density estimates.  Method (a) in the method in which individuals were used in the analysis in contrast to method (b) where groups were used in the analysis.

>
>
> Results
>
> I would like to understand how to read the reasults on the KS test and the CvM test. I have copied two outputs below the first is for gruped data and the second for the ungrouped. I understand from other posts that a p ≤0.05 like the one Ive got in both cases for the KS test tells me so strong eviudence of lack of fit can I suspect this is due to the spike at cero distance? Is my reading right? How can I read the CvM tests? I understand this last one gives emphasis to observations near distance cero.

The K-S test as well as the two variations of the CvM test all attempt to quantify the results shown in the QQ plots.  QQ plots allow a visual inspection of the discrepancy between the observed perpendicular distances and the distribution of those distances predicted by the detection function model.  The K-S test finds the largest departure between observed and predicted values and creates a probability value based on that largest distance.  The CvM tests in contrast, look at the cumulative departures at all distances (with the second variant giving greater emphasis to departures at small distances as you note).  Small p-values of these tests suggest that the discrepancies did not arise by chance alone and the small p-values place suspicion on the conjecture that the fitted detection function is a good fit to the data.

messages.body_plain:
Laura:

You need to make a judgement about the data you have.  You are trying to fit a model to the *process* that gave rise to the data, rather than fit every bump and valley of your data.  Do not be completely driven by goodness of fit and AIC scores.

Apply a smooth (continuously decreasing) function to your data.  You may choose to bin the distance out to 9m to account for the rounding problem.  You will present the histograms in your report and describe your understanding of them.  The goodness of fit statistics help you understand your data, but they should not drive incessant tinkering with data to achieve fit.

There are no easy solutions when data have a spike at zero; every remedy you employ will have an element of opinion involved.

messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] How even or uneven the coverage probability should be in simulated designs?
messages.body_plain:
Adrian:

Interesting questions, as always.

The simple answer is that evenness of coverage probability is subjective.  There is no objective measure of evenness, although Strindberg did look at some metrics in her thesis.  Think of the analogy of a QQ plot as a measure of goodness of fit.  How far can the QQ plot deviate from the 45-degree line before you decide your model does not fit your data?  That is a subjective judgement, which is why the K-S and CvM tests quantify the visual image shown in the QQ plot.

I would not use the range (max - min) as a measure of evenness.  My personal preference is to use the standard deviation of hit percentage as an index of evenness.  I can use this as a relative measure "does design A produce more even coverage than design B".

With the highly crenelated study area of Thomas et al. (2007), I don't doubt that very large numbers of simulations may be needed to get a reasonable assessment of coverage probability.

messages.body_plain:
Ralf:

This survey design is not great for several reasons:
- roads do not sample the study area in a random or representative manner,
- animals know where roads are situated and are either attracted or repulsed by roads, leading to non-uniform distribution of animals at all perpendicular distances from the roads, and
- you only have a single replicate transect; this defeats your ability to measure encounter rate variability between transects; this is a fundamental element in assessing your ability to extrapolate from the places you sampled to the places you did not sample.

Breaking the transect into smaller parts does not solve issues 1 and 2 and does not effectively resolve issue 3.

Each of those difficulties makes it challenging for you to make legitimate inferences about the number of game animals in your reserve.

The direct answer to your questions is the amount of effort associated with your (single) transect is the length of the transect multiplied by the number of visits; in your case 13x8=104km.  You should entertain the possibility that different species have different detection functions, so you should enter all species into the same Distance project and either analyse them separately, or treat species as a factor covariate or strata in modelling your detection function.   That way you can statistically assess whether species share or have distinct detection functions.  Consult

Marques, T.A., Thomas, L., Fancy, S.G. and Buckland, S.T. 2007.  Improving estimates of bird density using multiple covariate distance sampling.  The Auk 124, 1229-1243.

messages.body_plain:
Hi listfolk,

Updated versions of the mrds, Distance and dsm R packages are now
available on CRAN. Release notes for each are available at:

https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/mrds/releases/tag/CRAN-2.1.14

https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/Distance/releases/tag/CRAN-0.9.4

https://github.com/DistanceDevelopment/dsm/releases/tag/CRAN-2.2.9

respectively.

Note that thanks to an error pointed out by Phil Bouchet on this list,
the data in the dsm packages (Gulf of Mexico pantropical spotted
dolphins) has been updated to include corrected areas for prediction
cells and segments. This has also been reflected in the DSM vignette on
distancesampling.org <http://distancesampling.org> which you can find at
http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/mexico-analysis.html

These releases of mrds and dsm will become a part of the upcoming beta
release of Distance 7 (for Windows).

All the best,
--dave
